s01.text: A floating-point number needs three things. A sign, an exponent, and a mantissa.

s02.text: The exponent says how big or small the number can be. The mantissa says how finely you can pin it down.

s03.text: FP32 spends thirty-two bits on that. Eight for the exponent, twenty-three for the mantissa, one for the sign.

s04.text: Halve it and you halve the mantissa first. FP16 keeps five exponent bits and ten mantissa bits.

s05.text: Keep going and you hit the real problem. The exponent runs out of room before the mantissa does.

s06.text: FP8 splits the difference two ways. E4M3 has four exponent bits and three mantissa bits. E5M2 has five and two.

s07.text: E4M3 has more precision and less range. E5M2 has more range and less precision.

s08.text: Which one you want depends on whether you are storing a weight or an activation.

s09.text: Then there is the clever part. You can shrink it to four bits. One sign, two exponent, one mantissa.

s10.text: That is so little precision that one shared scale for a whole block of numbers would destroy them.

s11.text: So the format stores a small scale factor alongside the block, and that scale is different for every group of values.

s12.text: Four bits per number, and the block keeps its meaning.

s13.text: That is how four-bit weights survive at all. The scale saves what one mantissa bit cannot hold.
